clinicalPearls: Characterised by episodes of burning pain, erythema and increased warmth of the extremities, affecting the feet more often than the hands and usually bilateral and symmetrical.
Symptoms are provoked by heat, exercise and limb dependency and are relieved by cooling and elevation.
Patients often immerse the limbs in cold water for relief, which can cause maceration, non-healing wounds and immersion injury.
The primary (inherited) form is linked to gain-of-function mutations in SCN9A encoding the Nav1.7 sodium channel, with autosomal dominant inheritance and early onset.
Secondary erythromelalgia is most importantly associated with myeloproliferative neoplasms, particularly polycythaemia vera and essential thrombocythaemia.
Erythromelalgia due to thrombocythaemia responds dramatically to aspirin, whereas primary channelopathy-related disease typically does not.
There is considerable overlap with small-fibre neuropathy, and many patients have abnormal intraepidermal nerve fibre findings.
reference.pathophysiology: Erythromelalgia reflects a mismatch between skin metabolic demand and perfusion, with maldistribution of cutaneous blood flow and arteriovenous shunting that leaves the skin relatively hypoxic despite increased total flow, producing the red, hot, painful extremity. In the primary inherited form, gain-of-function mutations in the SCN9A gene alter the Nav1.7 voltage-gated sodium channel expressed in nociceptive and sympathetic neurons, lowering their firing threshold and causing hyperexcitability and neuropathic burning pain. Secondary forms arise from platelet-mediated microvascular occlusion in myeloproliferative disease or from other neuropathic and vasomotor disturbances.
additionalDifferentials: Raynaud phenomenon (opposite triggers and colour change)
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count with JAK2 mutation analysis to exclude a myeloproliferative neoplasm
SCN9A genetic testing when there is early onset or a family history
Small-fibre neuropathy assessment including skin biopsy for intraepidermal nerve fibre density and quantitative sensory testing
Thermography or skin temperature monitoring during an episode
Autoimmune and connective tissue disease screen
Review of medications known to provoke the condition
redFlags: Skin breakdown, ulceration or immersion injury from repeated cooling
Features of a myeloproliferative neoplasm such as thrombosis, splenomegaly or abnormal blood counts
Signs of secondary infection in macerated skin
reference.prognosis: The primary form is often lifelong and may be refractory to treatment, whereas secondary erythromelalgia usually improves when the underlying cause is addressed, and thrombocythaemic disease characteristically responds to aspirin.
pitfalls: Permitting prolonged cold-water immersion, which causes tissue damage and non-healing wounds.
Missing an underlying myeloproliferative neoplasm as a treatable cause.
Misdiagnosing an acute episode as cellulitis and giving unnecessary antibiotics.
Failing to recognise a heritable sodium-channelopathy in a child or young adult with a positive family history.
